where: lesson glance: Look 2 and shortcut text
what: Same inversion as nph: 'Look 2: PCO2 against pH. Opposite direction (pH down, CO2 down) -> metabolic. Same direction -> respiratory.' pH down + CO2 down is the same direction. Contradicts ROME and the app's own 'mixed' lesson wording.
fix: Change to 'Same direction (pH down, CO2 down; or pH up, CO2 up) -> metabolic. Opposite direction (pH down, CO2 up) -> respiratory.' Keep the wording identical to nph so the two lessons teach one rule.

where: lesson read6, question 1 ('In step 3, pH 7.30, PCO2 55, HCO3 18')
what: The question's gas is internally impossible. Henderson: [H+] = 24 x 55 / 18 = 73 nmol/L, which is pH 7.14, not 7.30 (HH: 6.1 + log(18 / 1.65) = 7.14). The lesson that teaches 'Step 1: is it real?' uses a gas that fails step 1, and interp() would flag it as 'Numbers do not fit together'.
evidence: node: interp({pH:7.30,pco2:55,hco3:18}) -> real step 'Numbers do not fit together' (diff > 10%).
fix: Use a consistent gas, e.g. 'pH 7.14, PCO2 55, HCO3 18' (or pH 7.20, PCO2 50, HCO3 19 -> HH 7.20). Add a test in tests/ that runs every lesson question gas with pH, PCO2 and HCO3 through the Henderson check.

where: lesson racid: 'Act on' paragraph and key 'NIV trigger (COPD)'
what: NIV threshold given as 'pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 45 mmHg (6 kPa)'. The UK guideline (BTS/ICS 2016, already in SRC as davidson16) says start NIV when pH < 7.35 and pCO2 > 6.5 kPa (about 49 mmHg) persist despite optimal medical therapy. For an MRCEM learner, 6.5 kPa is the expected answer. The 45 mmHg figure is the ERS/ATS one and is not labelled as such.
evidence: BTS/ICS 2016 (Davidson AC et al. Thorax 2016;71 Suppl 2); confirmed in Irish Thoracic Society NIV flashcard: 'NIV should be started when pH<7.35 and pCO2>6.5 kPa persist or develop despite optimal medical therapy' https://irishthoracicsociety.com/education/irish-thoracic-society-flashcards/18-niv
fix: Body: 'pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa (49 mmHg) persisting after optimal medical therapy (BTS/ICS 2016; ERS/ATS uses > 45 mmHg)'. Key: 'NIV (COPD, BTS)' = 'pH < 7.35, PCO2 > 6.5 kPa after 1 h of treatment'.

what: Summary says NIV when 'PaCO₂ > 45 (6 kPa)'. 45 mmHg is 6.0 kPa, and BTS/ICS 2016 (the cited guideline) uses PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa (≈ 49 mmHg). The body correctly says 6.5 kPa, so the summary contradicts the body and mislabels the BTS threshold.
evidence: c3.js:197 sum; body 'BTS: pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa'. Davidson AC et al. Thorax 2016;71 Suppl 2 (NIV: pH < 7.35 and PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa persisting after immediate maximal standard medical treatment).
fix: Change sum to: 'NIV when pH < 7.35 and PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa (≈ 49 mmHg) persist after maximal standard treatment (GOLD and many US sources use > 45 mmHg).'

what: Table headed 'Finding (BTS/SIGN 2019)' lists 'PCO₂ low, SpO₂ ≥ 92% → Acute severe'. BTS/SIGN does not define acute severe asthma by gas; it uses PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110, inability to complete sentences. A low PCO₂ is equally present in moderate attacks, so the row teaches a non-guideline criterion under a guideline label.
evidence: SIGN 158 / BTS 2019, Table 'Levels of severity of acute asthma exacerbations'. Rendered table: shots/T06-asthma-desk.png.
fix: Replace row with 'PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110, can't complete sentences (gas usually shows low PCO₂) → Acute severe'; add to the life-threatening row 'PEF < 33%, exhaustion, silent chest, altered consciousness'; add near-fatal 'or mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures'.

where: lesson dka · body 'What the gas tells you during treatment'
what: The potassium rule omits the key safety threshold: if K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L, give potassium and delay insulin (2024 consensus) / senior review and extra K⁺ (JBDS). 'K⁺ before insulin' alone does not tell the learner what to do with a low K⁺, a classic MRCEM/USMLE item.
evidence: 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus (Umpierrez et al., Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257–1275): replace K⁺ when < 5.0; if < 3.5 replace ~10 mmol/h and delay insulin until > 3.5. Summary in CCJM 2025;92:152 (https://www.ccjm.org/content/92/3/152). JBDS 02 2023: > 5.5 none, 3.5–5.5 40 mmol/L, < 3.5 senior review.
fix: Replace bullet with: 'Check K⁺ before insulin. K⁺ > 5.5 (JBDS) / > 5.0 (ADA): no K⁺ in fluids, recheck in 1–2 h. 3.5–5.5: add 40 mmol/L KCl. < 3.5: replace K⁺ and hold insulin until > 3.5 (senior review).' Add a 'K⁺ < 3.5' key number.

where: methb: question 'Oxygen therapy in methaemoglobinaemia…' explanation (c8.js XQ.methb also)
what: Explanation 'Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so the reading stays near 85%' gives the wrong mechanism. The ≈85% plateau is optical: MetHb absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm, driving the red/infrared ratio towards 1, which the oximeter maps to ≈85%. Oxygen does raise dissolved O2 (PaO2 210 in the example) but the pulse oximeter cannot see it.
evidence: Ash-Bernal 2004 (already cited); Barker SJ, Tremper KK, Anesthesiology 1989;70:112 (MetHb and pulse oximetry).
fix: Change to: 'MetHb absorbs red and infrared light equally, so the oximeter reads about 85% whatever the true saturation; extra oxygen raises PaO₂ but barely moves the reading.' Fix in both c3.js (lesson q) and c8.js XQ.methb.

where: methb: body 'Treat: … methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV…'
what: No warning about serotonin toxicity: methylene blue is a potent MAO-A inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, clomipramine, linezolid etc. This is a regulator-level warning and very relevant in overdose patients. Also missing: give over 5 minutes, may repeat once after 30–60 min, and lower thresholds (treat at lower MetHb) in anaemia, cardiac or lung disease.
evidence: FDA Drug Safety Communication 26/07/2011 (methylene blue and serotonergic drugs); Iolascon A, et al. Recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of methemoglobinemia. Am J Hematol 2021;96:1666–1678.
fix: Add bullet: 'Methylene blue is an MAO inhibitor: serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/SNRIs and other serotonergic drugs. Give 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min; repeat once after 30–60 min if needed. Treat at lower levels if anaemic or with cardiac or lung disease.' Add Iolascon 2021 to SRC and LSRC.methb.

what: The card 'NIV trigger (COPD): pH < 7.35, PaCO₂ > 45' disagrees with BTS/ICS 2016 (PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa ≈ 49 mmHg, after optimal medical therapy). The app's own COPD shift quotes 6.5 kPa.
evidence: Number flash card racid-2. BTS/ICS acute hypercapnic respiratory failure guideline 2016 (Thorax 71:ii1).
fix: Change it to 'pH < 7.35 and PaCO₂ > 6.5 kPa (≈ 49 mmHg) despite optimal medical therapy'.

what: Says 'PaO2 108 on air: normal ... A-a = 12'. For age 24 the app's own rule (A-a <= age/4 + 4) gives 10, and the Interpreter shows 'A-a = 12 (expected <= 10 for age 24)' next to 'Normal oxygenation'. The lesson calls it normal without saying why.
evidence: openLesson('read6') -> Open in the Interpreter; ox step text.
fix: Either change the gas so A-a <= 10 (e.g. PaO2 112) or add: 'A-a 12 is within a few mmHg of the expected 10; the rule is approximate, so this is normal.'

what: 'Winter's, 0.7 x HCO3 + 20, or 1-4-2-5' reads as if Winter's formula were 0.7 x HCO3 + 20. Winter's is 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 +/- 2 (acidosis); 0.7 x HCO3 + 20 is the alkalosis rule.
fix: 'Compensation. Metabolic acidosis: Winter's 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 +/- 2. Metabolic alkalosis: 0.7 x HCO3 + 20 +/- 5. Respiratory: 1-4 (acidosis) and 2-5 (alkalosis) per 10 mmHg.'

what: Worked gas has lactate 9.1 but the AG rise is about 18 (AG 30.2 corrected). The lesson's own approach says if lactate does not account for the rise, hunt for another anion, and the Interpreter says 'Lactate 9.1 accounts for about 50% of the gap rise' - yet the lesson gives no comment or clinical stem, so the learner cannot tell whether a second acid is intended.
evidence: node interp(hagma.ex): gap step 'Lactate 9.1 accounts for about 50% of the gap rise'.
fix: Either raise lactate to about 16 (pure lactic acidosis) or add a stem and a line: 'Lactate explains only half the gap: check ketones, creatinine, osmolar gap.'

what: 'PCO2 = last two digits of pH (pH 7.10-7.35)' fails at the low end. At pH 7.10 with PCO2 10, HCO3 = 3.0, Winter's predicts 12.5 +/- 2. The rule holds from about 7.15 to 7.35. Also 'HCO3 + 15 (HCO3 10-20)': at HCO3 20 it gives 35, but Winter's gives 38 +/- 2 (36-40).
evidence: Script: for pH 7.05-7.40, PCO2 = (pH - 7) x 100, HCO3 by HH, Winter's: off at 7.05, 7.10 and 7.40. HCO3 20 -> 35 vs 38.
fix: State 'pH about 7.15-7.35' (also in Look 3) and 'HCO3 + 15 for HCO3 about 8-18'.

what: 'Reflex tab: Level 1 ...' - there is no Reflex tab. Tabs are Today, Learn, Labs, Practice, Progress; Reflex is a Practice mode.
evidence: ui1.js quick buttons / ui2.js modes: reflex is a session mode.
fix: 'Practice -> Reflex: Level 1 until ...'. A deep link button to startSession('reflex') would be better.

what: 'Both values moving against the pH -> two disorders' is unclear: which values, and against what? The rule meant is 'PCO2 and HCO3 both moved in the direction that explains the pH' (as read6 step 3 says), or 'PCO2 and HCO3 moved in opposite directions'.
fix: 'If PCO2 and HCO3 both push the pH the same way (high CO2 + low HCO3, or low CO2 + high HCO3) -> two primary disorders.'

what: 'PCO₂ by Winter's' and 'VBG is enough' sit together, but Winter's is for arterial PCO₂. Venous PCO₂ runs ~5–8 mmHg higher, so a learner applying Winter's to the VBG PCO₂ will over-call respiratory acidosis (the worked VBG itself has PvCO₂ 17 vs Winter's 15.4 on measured values).
evidence: c3.js:136 body; worked example is sample 'v'.
fix: Add: 'Winter's applies to arterial PCO₂; on a VBG subtract ≈ 5 mmHg first, or use the trend.'

what: EXTRIP criteria are paraphrased loosely: 'hypoxaemia' should be 'new hypoxaemia needing supplemental oxygen'; pH ≤ 7.20 is a 'suggested' criterion without 'despite treatment'; 'failure of standard therapy' and the renal-impairment threshold (> 6.5 mmol/L / 90 mg/dL) are missing.
evidence: Juurlink 2015 Ann Emerg Med 66:165: recommended: level > 7.2 mmol/L (100 mg/dL); > 6.5 mmol/L with impaired kidney function; altered mental status; new hypoxaemia requiring O₂; failure of standard therapy. Suggested: > 6.5 (90 mg/dL); > 5.8 (80 mg/dL) with impaired kidney function; pH ≤ 7.20.
fix: Rewrite bullet with these exact criteria and units (mmol/L first, mg/dL in brackets).

what: Hook says 'High gap, no lactate…'. Ethylene glycol's metabolite glycolate falsely raises lactate on many blood gas analysers (lactate gap), so an EG patient can show a high lactate; the hook may falsely reassure.
evidence: Kraut & Mullins NEJM 2018;378:270 (cited) discusses falsely elevated lactate in EG poisoning.
fix: Add bullet: 'Ethylene glycol can falsely raise point-of-care lactate (glycolate interference); a gas lactate far above the lab lactate is a clue.' Soften hook to 'High gap that lactate and ketones do not explain…'.

what: Dialysis indications are vague ('high levels'); no EXTRIP numbers, no antidote doses, although the brief asks for drug doses to be checkable.
evidence: EXTRIP methanol (Roberts DM et al., Crit Care Med 2015;43:461–472): coma, seizures, new visual deficit, pH ≤ 7.15, persistent acidosis, AG > 24, methanol > 700 mg/L with fomepizole. EXTRIP EG (Ghannoum M et al., Kidney Int 2023): severe acidosis (pH ≤ 7.25–7.30), AKI, EG > 50 mmol/L or OG > 50.
fix: List EXTRIP criteria per alcohol and doses: fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV load then 10 mg/kg 12-hourly ×4 then 15 mg/kg (redose during dialysis); folinic acid 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) 4–6-hourly; thiamine 100 mg, pyridoxine 50 mg; ethanol target 100–150 mg/dL (≈ 22–33 mmol/L). Add EXTRIP refs to c5.js LSRC.toxalc2.

what: Worked gas has lactate 3.1 but AG 12.8 (corrected 12.3); a lactate of 3.1 should push the gap ~2 above baseline. Internally inconsistent for a lesson that teaches lactate.
fix: Set cl:101 (AG ≈ 14.8) or lac:1.8.

what: 'Lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L: screen for organ dysfunction' is odd: a raised lactate is itself a hypoperfusion marker; SSC 2021 recommends measuring lactate and guiding resuscitation to lower it. Key 'Septic shock lactate > 2 with vasopressors' drops 'despite adequate fluid resuscitation'.
evidence: Singer M et al. JAMA 2016;315:801 (Sepsis-3); Evans 2021 SSC.
fix: Bullet: 'Lactate > 2 suggests hypoperfusion: resuscitate and remeasure within 2–4 h, aiming for a fall (SSC 2021).' Key: '> 2 + vasopressors for MAP ≥ 65 despite fluids'.

what: 'Oral bicarbonate when HCO₃⁻ persistently below about 18–22 to slow progression' overstates the evidence. KDIGO 2024 suggests considering treatment at < 18 mmol/L and notes uncertain benefit for progression (BiCARB trial negative).
evidence: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline rec 3.10.1; BiCARB, BMC Med 2020.
fix: Rewrite: 'KDIGO 2024: consider treatment (oral bicarbonate or diet) when HCO₃⁻ < 18 mmol/L; the older 2012 threshold was < 22. Benefit for progression is uncertain; bone and muscle protection is the stronger rationale.'

where: co: sum 'assume cyanide too if lactate is above 8', key 'Lactate > 8 in smoke', body bullet
what: The validated threshold in fire victims is lactate > 10 mmol/L (Baud 1991: sens 87%, spec 94%, PPV 95% for blood CN > 40 µmol/L). The ≥ 8 cut-off comes from pure cyanide poisoning (Baud 2002), not smoke. 'Assume' is also stronger than the evidence.
evidence: Baud FJ, et al. N Engl J Med 1991;325:1761–1766 (confirmed via UMEM pearl #3156); Baud FJ, et al. Crit Care Med 2002;30:2044.
fix: Write: 'In smoke inhalation, lactate ≥ 10 mmol/L (some use ≥ 8) with coma, shock or arrest → suspect cyanide and give hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV (70 mg/kg in children).' Key: 'Lactate ≳ 8–10 in smoke'. Add baud91 to SRC/LSRC.co.

what: 'Persistently below about 10 mmHg after 20 minutes is a poor sign' lacks the ERC 2021 caveat that ETCO2 must not be used alone to stop resuscitation. Also no mention of avoiding hypoxaemia (ERC: avoid PaO2 < 8 kPa / 60 mmHg) alongside hyperoxia; the worked gas itself shows PaO2 72 on FiO2 1.0, which the body never discusses.
evidence: Soar J et al. ERC 2021 ALS, Resuscitation 2021;161:115 ('low ETCO2 after 20 min associated with poor outcome; do not use alone'). Nolan 2021 post-resuscitation: titrate to 94–98%, avoid hypoxaemia.
fix: Append: '…a poor sign, but never a reason on its own to stop.' Add bullet: 'Avoid hypoxaemia as much as hyperoxia: the example (PaO₂ 72 on FiO₂ 1.0, P/F 72) needs PEEP and a look for aspiration or oedema, not less oxygen.'

what: Explanation relies on 'expected ≈ 11 for a young adult' but neither stem gives an age (Q1 says only 'Overdose, room air, sea level'). The app's own rule age/4+4 needs the age.
fix: Q1 stem: 'Overdose, 28 years old, room air, sea level: PaCO₂ 80, PaO₂ 45. A–a?' Keep Q2 explanation: 'expected ≤ 11 (28/4 + 4)'.

what: PaCO2 78, PaO2 52 on air gives A–a exactly 0, which is physiologically implausible (a healthy young adult has 5–10) and weakens the teaching of 'normal A–a' (it looks like a contrived zero).
fix: Set ex.po2 to 45 (A–a 7, still normal for age 27).

what: Sedatives are in the title but nothing on benzodiazepines or flumazenil (not routinely recommended: seizure risk in mixed/TCA overdose and benzodiazepine dependence), and no naloxone dosing.
evidence: Lesson body (4 bullets, none on benzodiazepines).
fix: Add: 'Naloxone 100–400 micrograms IV titrated to breathing, not to full alertness (UK: 400 mcg IM/IV, repeat). Flumazenil is not routine: seizures in mixed or TCA overdose and in dependence.' Add a toxicology source (e.g. Boyer EW. Management of opioid analgesic overdose. N Engl J Med 2012;367:146–155).

where: opioid: q3 option 'Improve SpO₂ while hypoventilation worsens'
what: Supplemental O2 does not make opioid hypoventilation worse (that is the COPD/hypoxic-drive story). The point is that SpO2 masks rising CO2.
fix: Option: 'Keep SpO₂ normal while CO₂ keeps rising unseen'. Explanation: 'Oxygen hides hypoventilation from the oximeter; watch RR, ETCO₂ or a gas.'

what: Says 'cooling comes before investigation' but gives no method or target. For an ER doctor the actionable numbers are: cold-water immersion (or best available: ice-water towels, evaporative), cool to ≈ 38.5–39 °C within 30 minutes ('cool first, transport second'), stop at 38.5–39 to avoid overshoot. Also the definition should note that core temperature may be < 40 °C if cooling began pre-hospital.
evidence: Roberts WO et al. ACSM consensus 2023; Epstein & Yanovich NEJM 2019.
fix: Add a 'Cooling' bullet with the method, target and rate (≥ 0.15 °C/min with immersion), and to the definition: '(may be lower if cooling has already started)'.

where: heat: 'hyponatraemia in exertional hyponatraemia from overdrinking'
what: Tautological wording; the accepted term is exercise-associated hyponatraemia (EAH).
fix: 'Hyponatraemia in exercise-associated hyponatraemia (EAH) from drinking too much hypotonic fluid.'

what: HBO indications are listed as if settled. Evidence is mixed (Weaver 2002 RCT positive, Scheinkestel 1999 negative; Cochrane 2011 insufficient evidence), and severe acidosis (pH < 7.1) is a commonly listed criterion that is missing. Normal COHb values (non-smoker < 3%, smoker up to ~10%) are also absent, though the slip flags COHb > 3.
evidence: Buckley NA et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;CD002041; Weaver LK et al. N Engl J Med 2002;347:1057.
fix: Add: '…or severe acidosis (pH < 7.1). Evidence is mixed; discuss with the regional hyperbaric unit.' and 'Normal COHb < 3% (smokers up to 10%).'

where: methb: q 'Methylene blue is contraindicated in… G6PD deficiency'
what: G6PD deficiency is a relative contraindication (MB may be ineffective and cause haemolysis; low-dose MB is sometimes still used when deficiency is unknown or partial). 'Contraindicated' is acceptable for an exam answer but the body says it 'does not work', which is too absolute.
fix: Body: 'may not work and can cause haemolysis'. Question stem: 'Methylene blue should be avoided in…'.

where: preg: body 'Lower bicarbonate means less buffer: DKA in pregnancy is more rapid and can occur at lower glucose.'
what: Conflates two mechanisms. Less buffer explains faster acidosis; the lower glucose comes from fetoplacental glucose uptake, higher GFR (glycosuria) and accelerated starvation ketosis, not from the low bicarbonate.
fix: 'Lower bicarbonate means less buffer, so DKA develops faster; fetal glucose uptake means it can occur at near-normal glucose (euglycaemic DKA).'

where: preg: q 'Why aim for maternal SpO₂ of 95% or more?'
what: The 95% target is tested but never taught in the body.
fix: Add to Pregnancy list: 'Keep SpO₂ ≥ 95% (PaO₂ > 70 mmHg): the fetus sits on the steep part of its own curve.'

what: There is duplication across modules. The clin lesson 'Normal variants: pregnancy and altitude' teaches altitude (Riyadh, Abha, acetazolamide), which sp-alt now covers in more depth. It also teaches the pregnancy baseline and 'PaCO2 40 = tiring asthma', and sp-pregem repeats both. preg q[0] (asthmatic PaCO2 41) and sp-pregem Q1 (ventilated, PaCO2 40) test the same fact. The two lessons don't contradict each other (27–32 vs 30–32; HCO3 18–21 vs ≈ 20), but a learner meets the same content twice, about 60 lessons apart.
fix: Rename preg to 'Pregnancy: normal values' and move its Altitude <h3> block (Riyadh/Abha lines) into sp-alt, which lacks the local cities. Replace its q[1] with a pregnancy item, e.g. 'pH 7.44, PCO2 30, HCO3 20 at 30 weeks: normal for pregnancy'. In sp-pregem, open with 'Baseline: see Pregnancy: normal values' and change Q1 to a ventilator-setting decision, e.g. 'PaCO2 40 on the ventilator: raise the minute ventilation'.

what: 'Open this case in the Interpreter with the button below' - on tablet and desktop the button sits in the right-hand aside ('Worked gas' card), not below.
fix: '...with the Open in the Interpreter button on the worked gas card.'

where: original lesson questions in c2/c3 (first two per lesson)
what: The correct option is the longest by 40% or more in 20 of 95 questions, almost all in the hand-written first two questions: nlac Q1, nbe Q1, vbg Q3, read6 Q1-Q3, malk Q1-Q2, racid Q2, ralk Q1, mixed Q2-Q3, nagma Q2, glance Q2-Q4 and others. Test-wise learners can guess them.
evidence: Script over L: compare option lengths (list in this note).
fix: Lengthen distractors to match, e.g. nlac Q1: 'Lactic acidosis fully explains the gap'; 'Repeat lactate before anything else'; malk Q2: 'Vomit contains a large amount of sodium'.

where: pe q[0], diarr q[1], renalfail q[0]
what: Three questions have only two options (Yes/No, Positive/Negative), a 50% guess rate; they score the same as four-option items.
fix: Convert to four options (e.g. PE: 'Normal A–a excludes PE' / 'Normal PaO₂ excludes PE' / 'No ABG finding excludes PE' / 'Respiratory alkalosis confirms PE').

what: 'ADH' is used without expansion; in an acid–base app ADH normally means antidiuretic hormone (used in kidney lessons).
evidence: sum 'Block ADH early with fomepizole'; hook 'block ADH now'.
fix: Write 'alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)' at first use, or 'block alcohol dehydrogenase'.

what: Uses 'massive PE'; ESC 2019 terminology is 'high-risk PE' (with intermediate-high/low).
fix: Write 'High-risk (massive) PE' in body and key.

what: Key 'Urine Cl⁻ < 20' has no unit.
fix: '< 20 mmol/L'.

what: Body says established sepsis often has PCO₂ below Winter's (added respiratory alkalosis), but the worked gas is an exactly compensated HAGMA (PCO₂ 27, Winter's 27.8), so the example does not show the pattern taught.
evidence: interp label 'High anion gap metabolic acidosis'.
fix: Use e.g. pCO₂ 23, pH 7.38 (HH: 6.1+log(13.2/0.69)=7.38) to show HAGMA + respiratory alkalosis, or add a caption saying which stage the example is.

where: arrest: q 'Ideal PaCO₂ after ROSC?' options
what: Options '25–30', '35–45', '50–60' have no units; with kPa as an option in Settings they are ambiguous.
fix: Use '35–45 mmHg (4.7–6.0 kPa)' style labels or route through the unit formatter.

what: The worked DKA gas has no K⁺, but the lesson's first treatment point is 'K⁺ before insulin'.
fix: Add K⁺ 5.6 to the worked gas and one line under it: 'K⁺ 5.6: no potassium in the first bag; recheck in 1–2 h'.

where: lessons hagma, nagma, malk, racid, ralk, mixed (ex)
what: Six of the seven worked gases have no clinical stem; only read6 tells a story. A gas without a patient teaches pattern-matching, not interpretation.
evidence: render.json: the lEx card shows the slip only.
fix: Add ex.stem (one line, e.g. '58-year-old, septic shock, on noradrenaline') and render it above the slip in renderLesson (ui1.js).

what: Examples teach hypo/hyperkalaemia but have no K⁺. The engine already accepts k.
fix: Add k: dka 5.8 (high at presentation despite total-body deficit), vomit 2.8, diarr 3.0.

what: No doses or fluid steps although this is a shift tool.
fix: Add JBDS/ADA box: 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid 1 L in 1 h (500–1000 mL/h for 2–4 h, ADA), FRIII 0.1 units/kg/h, add 10% glucose at glucose < 14 mmol/L (JBDS) / 5–10% dextrose < 13.9 (ADA), and note JBDS acidosis criterion HCO₃⁻ < 15 vs consensus < 18.

what: Practical alkalinisation details missing.
fix: Add: 8.4% sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg bolus then infusion, keep K⁺ ≥ 4 (alkalinisation fails if hypokalaemic), blood pH not above ~7.55; bicarbonate bolus before any intubation; salicylate can cause pseudohyperchloraemia (low/negative AG) on some analysers.

what: No resuscitation numbers.
fix: Add SSC 2021: 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 h for hypoperfusion (weak), balanced crystalloids preferred, noradrenaline first line, target MAP 65, capillary refill time as an adjunct.

what: Add bicarbonaturia pearl.
fix: Early/active vomiting: urine Na⁺ and K⁺ high (bicarbonaturia) while urine Cl⁻ stays low; paradoxical aciduria in pyloric stenosis.

what: Exceptions.
fix: Add villous adenoma and congenital chloride diarrhoea as diarrhoea causes of metabolic alkalosis.

what: Isopropanol pearl.
fix: Isopropanol: nitroprusside ketone test positive (acetone) but BHB normal, no acidosis, high osmolar gap.

what: Doubt to verify: BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 (NG245) replaced the chronic sections of SIGN 158; acute severity criteria are still from SIGN 158 (2019).
fix: Confirm and phrase the label as 'BTS/SIGN 2019 (SIGN 158), acute section'.

what: ESC risk stratification link.
fix: Add a line: lactate > 2 and RV dysfunction feed ESC risk strata; ABG does not enter Wells/Geneva/PERC (PERC uses SpO₂ ≥ 95%).

what: The interpreter labels the pregnancy example 'chronic respiratory alkalosis'; the lesson should say so explicitly and teach that this is the expected reading.
evidence: interp(preg ex) → 'Primary respiratory alkalosis; chronic, renally compensated'.
fix: Add a sentence: 'The interpreter will call this compensated respiratory alkalosis; in pregnancy that is normal.' Longer term: a 'pregnant' toggle in the interpreter that shifts reference ranges.

what: Add temp 41.5 to the heat worked gas so the slip shows temperature and the alpha-stat point is visible.
fix: ex.temp=41.5 and a line in the slip: 'reported at 37 °C (alpha-stat)'.

what: Occupational angle for a Qiddiya OH/ER doctor: methylene chloride (paint stripper) is metabolised to CO with delayed and prolonged COHb rise.
fix: Add to Sources bullet: 'methylene chloride paint strippers (CO made in the liver, rises late)'.
